name: Lena Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Lena, thank you for doing this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the supermarket on the market square, the mid-size one, and I split my time between the deli counter and the tills. Mornings I slice ham and cheese, weigh olives, do the hot chicken for lunch, and afternoons I'm usually on till four. I'm still learning the deli, last week I sliced a whole salami too thick and the supervisor made me sell it as a reduced pack.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the counter more than the till, because people talk to you about what they're cooking. I've got a regular who buys exactly a hundred grams of blue cheese every Friday for her husband. The hard part is the cleaning at close, the slicer takes forty minutes, and the pay doesn't really cover the town's rents.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Sami, he drives a parcel van for one of the big delivery firms. We rent a small terrace on Station Road. I use AI apps sometimes, for a recipe or for fixing my CV, but not every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, a bit of help with boring stuff and that's it. Okay, that sounds pretty realistic actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like the self-checkouts, a bit useful and a bit annoying, nothing to panic about. At work we'd moan about the new screens if they put any in. I don't post much, maybe a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life stays the same, which isn't great either, because we have about a month of rent between us and that's it. My wage is the lowest grade, and Sami's van job pays per parcel, so a slow week hurts. Nothing here makes it worse, but nothing makes it better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the food hygiene level two certificate the store offers, because the deli needs it and it gets me a few pence more an hour. I'd ask to be on the counter full time instead of half tills. I'd keep the twenty a month we put aside for Sami's van insurance excess, in case he crashes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Just that steady low worry you get when there's no buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if a bad month came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the energy bill, because they let you go into arrears a bit. Rent never, and the phones never, because Sami needs his for work. We did that once in January and it took till April to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the counter rather than the till?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the till is the bit they keep replacing with self-checkouts, you can see it happening. Nobody's made a machine that tells you which ham is nicest for a sandwich. The counter feels safer and I like it more.

say: AI is like the **self-checkouts**: a bit useful, a bit annoying, nothing to **panic** about.
We'd moan about any **new screens** at work.
think: Life stays the same, with about **a month of rent** saved between us.
**Sami's van** pay is per parcel, so slow weeks hurt.
do: Take the store's **food hygiene** level two certificate for a small raise.
Ask to work the **deli counter** full time instead of tills.
Keep putting **twenty a month** aside for the van insurance excess.
feel: Fine, with a steady **low worry** about having **no buffer**.
S0.quote: Nobody's made a machine that tells you which ham is nicest for a sandwich.
fieldNote: Already reads the **till** as the part of her job being replaced.
Household runs on **two insecure wages**, one paid per parcel.
Once fell behind on **energy bills** for three months after a bad January.

steps.text: Take the store's level two food hygiene certificate
Ask to move to the deli counter full time
Keep saving twenty a month for the van insurance excess

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. Ordering, booking, answering customers. That sounds like Sami's work more than mine, the routes and the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say most of us on the shop floor are fine for now, it's the office and the call centres. I'd tell friends to look at where robots are slow and go there. Online I'd probably share something about it, but not get into fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm more worried about Sami than me. His route planning, his customer messages, all the app stuff will get smarter and they'll squeeze more parcels into his day. My counter's safe for a few years, but if my boyfriend's delivery pay drops, we drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the hygiene certificate and then ask about the bakery side too, so I'm useful on two counters. I'd get Sami to look at a bus or lorry licence while his firm still pays some training. And we'd try to build up to two months of rent, putting his tips away instead of spending them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, yeah. It's not my job I'm counting, it's our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your counter's safe for a few years. What would change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they start doing pre-packed everything, so there's no counter at all. The big out-of-town store already did that last year. That's a decision by a planner on a screen, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sami take it if you suggested a lorry licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, because he likes being on his own in the van. But he's practical, like me. If I showed him the numbers he'd do it.

say: Shop floor staff are fine **for now**; it's offices and **call centres**.
I'd tell friends to go where **robots are slow**.
think: I'm more worried about **Sami** than me; his app will squeeze in **more parcels**.
do: Learn the **bakery** counter as well as the deli.
Get Sami to look at a **lorry licence** while his firm pays training.
Save his **tips** to build up to **two months** of rent.
feel: **Anxious**, counting **our rent** rather than her own job.
S1.quote: My counter's safe for a few years, but if my boyfriend's delivery pay drops, we drop.
fieldNote: Shifts the worry to her boyfriend's **delivery job**, more exposed to thinking AI than hers.
Sees **pre-packed** counters as a planner's decision that could end her role.
A **practical couple** who decide by looking at numbers.

steps.text: Learn the bakery counter as well as the deli
Get Sami to apply for a lorry licence paid by his firm
Put Sami's tips aside to reach two months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, and robots 2031. That's fast. That's Sami's job in two years and mine in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need some kind of safety net, not just for us but for everyone in delivery and shops. I'm not political really, but you can't have half the town out of work at once. At work I think everyone would go very quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Sami's app job goes first, because if AI plans everything, the next thing is vans that drive themselves. Then the counter goes when the robots come. So we'd have maybe three years of my wage alone, and my wage doesn't pay the rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd move somewhere cheaper first, maybe back near my parents in the next town where rent is less. I'd look at care or hospital catering, work with real people in it, and use the AI apps to find what's hiring. I'd stop the twenty a month for van insurance and put everything into a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, the kind where you check your bank app twice a day. I've never been that person, and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sami the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boyfriend we're a team, we'll work it out, and then I'd cry in the bathroom. He'd be quiet for a few days, that's how he is. Then he'd start looking at lorry jobs anyway, even though lorries drive themselves too by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work with real people. Is that about safety or about what you like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I like people, and people want people when they're sick or old. I'm hoping that's the last thing a robot takes over.

say: We need a **safety net** for delivery and shop workers.
You can't have **half the town** out of work at once.
At work everyone would go **very quiet**.
think: **Sami's job** goes first, then vans that **drive themselves**.
We'd have maybe **three years** on my wage alone.
My wage alone **doesn't pay** the rent.
do: Move near her **parents** in the next town where rent is less.
Look at **care or hospital catering**, using AI apps to search.
Put the **insurance money** into a cushion instead.
feel: **Scared**, checking the **bank app** twice a day.
S2.quote: I'd tell my boyfriend we're a team, we'll work it out, and then I'd cry in the bathroom.
fieldNote: Expects her boyfriend's income to go **within two years**; that sets her mood.
Plans to cry **in the bathroom** after reassuring him, a telling private detail.
Moves towards **people-facing work** as both preference and safety.

steps.text: Move near her parents where rent is cheaper
Apply for hospital catering or care jobs
Search job sites for care openings using AI apps
Redirect the van insurance money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. Okay, that's more time to get a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but people should start now, not in 2030. I'd tell the younger girls on tills to get a qualification. I'd keep it practical, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives Sami time to switch, maybe to a mechanic or a job fixing the delivery robots. And for me, the counter lasts till about 2034, so I could do a proper course in the evenings. It's still tight because we can't really pay for two people to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time catering course at the college next September, because hospital and care kitchens will still need cooks for a while. Sami would do a mechanic apprenticeship if one comes up, even on lower pay. We'd put off getting a dog and a bigger place until one of us is on better money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but okay. More like when you're planning a move than when you've lost your keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you cover Sami's lower pay during an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick up extra till shifts on Sundays, they pay a bit more. We'd cut the takeaway on Fridays and the streaming. It'd be a lean two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help with any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit, to plan the money and to practise for interviews. I'm not a big fan, but it's useful for that kind of thing. I'd want to see it working for my friends first though.

say: There's **time**, but start now, not in 2030.
I'd tell the younger till girls to get a **qualification**.
think: Five years gives **Sami** time to switch to **mechanic** work.
The **counter** lasts till about 2034, enough for an evening course.
do: Start a **catering course** next September for care kitchens.
Put off a **dog and bigger place**.
S3.quote: Hospital and care kitchens will still need cooks for a while.
fieldNote: Plans as a **couple**: one studies while the other covers the gap.
Uses AI cautiously, for **budgeting and interviews**, after seeing it work for friends.
Delays small **life plans**, like a dog and a bigger home.

steps.text: Start a part-time catering course next September
Work extra Sunday till shifts to cover Sami's apprenticeship
Put off getting a dog and a bigger place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's a lot of time, I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out by this one. At work I'd say do your courses now and don't wait. To friends I'd say it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think we'd be alright, if we actually do what we say. My worry is that ten years makes us lazy, and money's still tight in the meantime. The rent goes up every year whether there's AGI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the hygiene certificate this year and the catering course over two years, at a pace we can afford. Sami would get a mechanic qualification before 2030. We'd try to get to three months of savings so we can think about having kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit of a niggle. More about rent than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does the timeline change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd want kids before I'm thirty-five, so before it hits. But I'd want one of us on a steady job first. It's a race, kind of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If prices kept going up faster than our wages, like this year. That would push everything back, not the robots. That's the boring truth.

say: There's **no excuse** for anyone to be caught out by this one.
I'd tell people at work to do their **courses now**.
think: We'd be **alright** if we actually do what we say.
**Rent** goes up every year whether there's AGI or not.
do: Do the **hygiene certificate** now and catering over two years.
Help Sami get a **mechanic qualification** before 2030.
Save **three months** so they can think about kids.
S4.quote: Rent goes up every year whether there's AGI or not.
fieldNote: Robots feel distant here, but **rising rent** keeps her anxious about money.
Ties the **children** decision to one of them getting a steady job.
Worries ten years could make the couple **lazy**.

steps.text: Take the catering course over two years
Save three months of costs before having children
Plan to have children before she turns thirty-five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both our jobs go in a few years and we've got a month of rent. What would help is cheap courses at night and some help with rent while you retrain. Even a guarantee that the store tells us a year ahead would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. A lot of old people only come in for the chat at the counter. If that goes, it's not just us who lose something.

headlineQuote: A lot of old people only come in for the chat at the counter.
portrait: Lena is 27 and splits her days between the **deli counter** and tills at a market-square supermarket.
She lives with **Sami**, a parcel driver, and they have about a **month of rent** saved.
She's **practical**, uses AI now and then, and plans as a **couple**.
Her worry follows **Sami's job** first, which is more exposed to AI than her counter work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both their jobs go within a few years on one month saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap night courses**, help with **rent** while retraining, and a year's notice from the store.
